item.title: Techno-Aquarium in the Style of the Infernal Abode: Launching a Local LLM Qwen 2.5 14B on a Home PC for an Interactive Website
item.description:
Today, no one is surprised by neural networks anymore – they are all anyone talks about. Whether it's video, text, or code generation. You have to look closely at the screen to understand: is this a real photo or AI work? People are actively setting up local neural networks at home and at work. So, I decided not to fall behind. Why? Because I can. Or I want to see if I can. For some kind of self-realization, it's interesting to go through this path. Just setting up a local AI on a PC is not interesting. I wanted to create something tangible, something different from a simple chatbot. The idea arose to 'settle' a neural network on a website, give it a character, grant it authority within the site. To simulate a real digital pseudo-life, a kind of digital aquarium, in which the Mistress of the INFERNUM project lives. Read more

item.title: [Translation] Development Flaw? Or Where is All This Productivity Growth Thanks to AI
item.description:
It would seem that the magic AI pill has already been invented, and it's time for all developers to produce three to four times more quality code. So why isn't this happening? Perhaps we should measure how diligently they are typing on their keyboards, take quantitative indicators from the DORA framework... and still not understand what's wrong. What about the SPACE framework? Something is missing again. Perhaps we should look both wider and deeper simultaneously. A developer is not a spherical horse in a vacuum: they communicate with colleagues, search for documentation, wait for management approvals, and all this takes time and effort, leaving none for writing code. To account for hidden chronophages and bottlenecks, DORA and SPACE should be supplemented with DevEx metrics, and then, perhaps, the puzzle will come together. We will analyze which metrics are responsible for what and how AI tools are changing the measurement of DevEx in 2026. Details are under the cut. Read more

item.title: [Translation] 600 Billion Tokens Later: How We Managed AI Agents While Decompiling a Shooter
item.description:
For three months, AI agents decompiled a popular first-person shooter, and we from the community managed them. Our goal was not to prove it was possible, but to achieve an accurate and stable C++ reconstruction of the game. Result: 99% of functions were restored, 83% of them match the original byte-for-byte, and the game runs without noticeable bugs. By my estimate, this took 600-700 billion tokens. But the article is not about the game, but about orchestrating autonomous agents: how to set up the infrastructure and harness to get quality results from agents for months, and why all this doesn't work without objective automatic verification. Read on

item.title: How AI is changing support: what remains of a ticket
item.description:
Since the late 1980s, when the first ticket tracking systems and the first version of ITIL appeared, the ticket has remained the main unit of work for technical support. Now this accounting scheme has to be revised, because AI agents are already performing actions in several systems at once: unlocking accounts, granting access, restarting services. We analyze what this leads to, what remains of a request when there is no one to take it for work, and how to measure support then. Read more

item.title: Why AI Agents Need Their Own Languages and Whether They Can Be Read
item.description:
⊕ = agreement, ⊖ = disagreement. This is what one of the simplest inter-agent "languages" from a selection of social network posts for Moltbook agents looks like. It resembles an agreement in a chat to respond with a plus and minus to save tokens. It would seem there's nothing criminal about it. But in the same selection, there's Symbiotica – a language where 26 Latin letters are replaced by glyphs from several scripts. Five letters have two variants. The choice between them encodes a bit (0 or 1) and forms a separate bit string. The visible text is read according to a correspondence table, like a cipher. But there's a second layer, carrying additional information that a random observer won't see, even if they have the table at hand. Read more

item.title: Hypothesis Playground: How to Know I'm Not Building a Useless Feature?
item.description:
AI has taught us to come up with hypotheses faster than we can test them. The bottleneck has shifted from idea generation to pre-launch testing. Unfortunately, this is as expensive as ever. The conclusion is that the business that gets more hypotheses to a useful impact wins. Of course, a $20/month gadget can churn out a seemingly perfect hypothesis from any context – as beautiful and precise as it is random and useless. I myself launched features based on such hypotheses until it cost several teams and a promotion budget. Hypothesis generation has accelerated, but testing remains the same as in 2020. Try saying "let's test first" out loud, and you'll be labeled a laggard, a person from the past, a Luddite. In this article, I'll explain what a hypothesis playground looks like in action: how the system is structured, how the orchestrator manages tasks, where the data comes from, why everything is set up this way, and what problems the playground solves. Read on.

item.title: AI Enhances CT Scans: Smart Tomo Engine Weekly Digest
item.description:
Today, computed tomography solves far more tasks than just visualizing an object's internal structure. In medicine, it's crucial to reduce radiation exposure and gain more information about tissues; in industry, to inspect complex objects without disassembly or destruction; and in scientific research, to work with non-standard imaging geometries and complex data types. Smart Engines develops technologies that expand CT capabilities at the level of reconstruction and data analysis algorithms. During Smart Tomo Engine Week, we discussed and demonstrated how our developments help reduce radiation load, determine the composition of the scanned object, obtain more information about soft tissues, perform non-destructive testing of complex products, and create portable tomographic systems. We've gathered the highlights from Smart Tomo Engine Week in one digest 👇 Read more

item.title: A Chat That Doesn't Make Things Up: 43 Hypotheses, Four Measurement Errors, and One Honest Wall
item.description:
The idea was simple and not new: large language models have two unpleasant properties—they cost money for every response and store tens of gigabytes of weights in memory, and they can confidently write things that don't exist anywhere. I wanted to build a system where the answer is selected from existing text, not generated: the corpus lies on disk as files, candidates are found by ordinary code, and a neural network judge only selects a string and verifies it. The judge is a classifier with typed primitives: 'choose one of the options,' 'is this true?', 'rate on a scale.' It doesn't write text at all. The answer is a verbatim quote with a source, and the system cannot invent a phrase that isn't in the corpus by design. Read more

item.title: A Call from Security: For Humans and Machines
item.description:
"Hello, this is the bank's security service..." – after that, it all goes according to script: authority, urgency, isolation ("don't hang up"), channel substitution. The exact same construct works against AI assistants: the zero-click prompt injection EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) in Microsoft 365 Copilot and the July 2026 incident with autonomous agents in the Hugging Face infrastructure, which no one hacked – they convinced themselves. The reason is one and architectural: neither humans nor language models have a separation between "data" and "instructions" at the input, and the difference between us is only the ability to exit the conversation. Meanwhile, the list of levers – false authority, artificial urgency, isolation from verification, channel substitution, social proof, step-by-step escalation – is the same for an accountant, a pensioner, a schoolchild, and an autonomous agent. It hasn't changed for centuries, only the scenery has. I'll break down why a phone scammer and prompt injection in LLMs are the same song, and what this implies for educating people. Read more

item.title: AI Benchmark Half-Life Halved: 19 Months Instead of 38
item.description:
In May, I submitted OenoBench, a wine benchmark for language models, to NeurIPS. During discussions with reviewers, a question arose that neither I nor they had a basis for: what result at release is sufficient for a new benchmark, and how long will it last? To answer this, I collected data on 224 benchmarks reported between 2018 and 2026 by nine labs: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI, DeepSeek, Alibaba, Moonshot, and Mistral. For each, I found its birth date and, if it had passed, its death date—the moment the benchmark can no longer distinguish top models: the leader achieves 90% or human-level performance, or the creators themselves declare the set saturated or broken. From these dates, I calculated the half-life: the time it takes for half of the benchmarks to die. Key findings: The benchmark half-life is 23 months. For those released before 2023, it was 38 months; for those released later, it's 19 months. The estimate accounts for benchmarks still alive, so the short history of new ones doesn't distort it. New benchmarks are not easier than old ones; models are simply faster. The initial gap to the ceiling is the same, but models cross it twice as fast. Every seventh new benchmark dies not because of models, but due to its own defects. For agentic environments, this is the cause of nearly half of all deaths. Below is how I calculated this and how long, based on this data, OenoBench itself will last. The dataset, codebook, and scripts are publicly available, with links at the end. Read more

item.title: Half a year without writing code by hand. I calculated what happened to bugs
item.description:
My name is Igor Simakov, I am a team lead, I manage two teams. These are two classic product teams that have everyone needed for the full development cycle, from discovery to delivery. I myself am a backend developer with ten years of experience and have not written code by hand since March 2026. Then I implemented practices in the teams and switched everyone to agent development: QA, backend, and frontend. So my teams have not been writing code by hand for six months. I decided to dig into what's happening and analyzed all the bugs of the two teams over the year, 268 of them. As it turned out, the bugs are not new, they existed before the agents. But now it has become more noticeable: we have started delivering three times more code, and noticeably more defects have started slipping through. Mostly these are under-the-hood, engineering, i.e., technical defects. Read more
